newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU budget pact seen test of Franco-German alliance.
newsitem.headline: EMU budget pact seen test of Franco-German alliance.

text.p: A budget stability pact designed to ensure spending discipline inside a single European currency, is shaping up to be the first critical test of the Franco-German alliance on economic and monetary union.

The new French Socialist government wasted no time on Monday in declaring its unhappiness with the painstakingly put together accord, one that is seen by the European Union as essential to the euro's credibility.

French Socialist Party spokesman Francois Hollande told Reuters Financial Television that the government did not want sanctions included in the so-called stability and growth pact, hammered out by European leaders last December and due for final approval later this month at a summit in Amsterdam.
"We want to be sure that sanctions will not be applied if the main objectives are not reached," Hollande said without elaborating further.
Under the pact, governments inside EMU would be penalised if they allowed their annual budget deficits to rise above three percent of Gross Domestic Product.

Although the agreement is considered by many to be a watered-down version of the initial blueprint proposed by Germany, it is an element of the EMU process which many believe enhances the project's ultimate success.
To reopen negotiations now could create a sharp rift between Bonn and Paris, the consequences of which analysts say is nearly impossible to gauge.
"This is significant in the sense that it is the first substantial difference between Germany and France over EMU," said Martin Brookes, economist at Goldman Sachs in London.
"It could potentially unsettle public opinion in Germany if there is a sense that the politicians in France are attempting to wrestle control over EMU away from the bankers."
In its election manifesto, the Socialist party laid down various conditions for the euro, including a European economic government to counterbalance an independent central bank.

The sharp differences in philosophy between the new French regime and the ousted centre-right have prompted speculation of increased tensions with Bonn at a time when there are growing divisions within Germany over proceeding with EMU on purely political grounds.

EU diplomats reacted cautiously to the Socialist warning, with several saying it was too early to tell how committed the French government would be on revisiting the budget pact. Some wondered whether they were merely posturing.
But several said it would be hard to imagine a scenario which saw the 15-nation bloc return to the bargaining table.

"The agreement was reached with such difficulty and it was so finely balanced that a I find it difficult to believe there is any willingness of any of the partners to reopen things again," said an EU diplomat.

Analysts noted that while the pact is an improvement over the existing EU procedure that sanctions governments with slack finances, the number of loopholes in the revised accord makes it unlikely that a government would ever be fined.

One important clause, fought over into the early hours of the morning during the EU summit in Dublin last December, was a definition of the economic circumstances that would allow a government to escape penalties.
Although the new French government may find the existing pact too stringent, analysts say a closer look at the details might prove that their concerns are ill-founded.
"The primary drawback of the whole thing is that there are enough loopholes to allow deficits above three percent of GDP without any penalties," said one London economist.
